extracted.intended_audience: community members, advocates, and residents seeking to file environmental justice / Title VI complaints with EPA
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for drafting and submitting an EPA civil-rights (Title VI and related) complaint alleging discriminatory environmental harms, including who to complain about, what to include, timing, and alternative paths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complain about the right entity or entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Your complaint has to say who’s causing the problem. EPA investigates complaints about recipients of EPA financial assistance (grants, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the issue involves a new or expanding industrial facility you will likely need to name the government agency issuing permits rather than the facility owner because the complaint process stems from laws banning discrimination by federal funding recipients. Many state/local agencies, tribal governments, universities and companies receive EPA grants or contracts; you can ask EPA or the organization if it’s a current funding recipient or search USAspending.gov (downloadable spreadsheets list EPA funding recipients). If there’s no responsible organization receiving EPA funds, consider complaining to a different federal agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline the discrimination you’re alleging (protected bases)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s Office of External Civil Rights Compliance takes complaints that allege discrimination based on: race; color; national origin (including limited English proficiency); sex; disability; age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additionally, EPA will consider complaints alleging intimidation or retaliation that violates its nondiscrimination regulation. If the environmental issue doesn’t involve discrimination, the civil-rights office may forward it to a regional office—contact the regional office directly in such cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness — file within 180 days
rubrics_metrics.description: A complaint must arrive within 180 days of the most recent act of alleged discrimination; EPA could, in theory, make an exception for good cause, but don’t count on that.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public Integrity found one in 10 rejected complaints marked “untimely.” Examples of actions that start the clock include permit approvals or failures to provide interpreters at public meetings. Don’t let additional research push you past the deadline; you can always provide more information after filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory core elements: funding recipient, discrimination, timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: The three categories — funding recipient, discrimination, and timeliness — are mandatory parts of a complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make sure at minimum that you’re complaining about a recipient of EPA funding within 180 days of an alleged discriminatory action they took. Many complaints are rejected for failing to identify a funding recipient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include identity and contact information; no anonymous complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: Include your name, signature (electronic is fine) and contact information when you file. The office doesn’t investigate anonymous complaints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can write your complaint in the language you know best; EPA’s manual says the civil-rights office “will take all necessary steps to ensure that persons who have limited English proficiency can participate meaningfully in its complaint process.”

rubrics_metrics.name: How to submit — email and mailing address
rubrics_metrics.description: Email your complaint to Title_VI_Complaints@epa.gov or mail it to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Office of External Civil Rights Compliance, Mail code 2310A, 1200 Pennsylvania Avenue, NW, Washington, DC 20460.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise can work; include documentation and be specific
rubrics_metrics.description: A concise email laying out the issues can be as successful as a long report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write up the facts as clearly as possible, be specific, and include documentation if you can. Examples include using EJScreen data to compare demographics and exposures. Read prior complaints for examples (both long lawyer-filed complaints and short letters have prompted investigations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mention federal law (Title VI and other statutes) — optional but helpful
rubrics_metrics.description: Environmental justice complaints to EPA involving race, color, or national origin are part of a process authorized by Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You don’t need to mention Title VI when you file, but it doesn’t hurt. EPA’s process also incorporates laws banning disability, sex, or age discrimination, so cite those other laws (for example, Title IX for sex discrimination in education programs) if relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand likely outcomes and remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA can withhold funding from recipients if it finds discrimination and cannot obtain compliance, but EPA has never taken that step; more likely is EPA negotiating an agreement with the recipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA’s regulation requires seeking cooperation and attempting informal resolution when possible. You can ask to be looped in on resolution efforts and inquire about entering alternative dispute resolution (ADR) with the recipient; some directly negotiated agreements have been more substantive than EPA’s negotiated deals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request specific remedies or relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain what results you want to see — what remedies would address the problems you’re facing? Would changing an agency’s process help?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noting desired remedies in your complaint can be a good strategy. Example: the NAACP complaint includes an eight-point list under “Relief Requested.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the type of discrimination: intentional vs disparate impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether you’re alleging intentional discrimination (the decision-maker meant to discriminate) or disparate impact (a neutral decision with discriminatory effects); either can qualify under federal policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It’s helpful to include examples that back up your assertions. Remember the 180-day deadline and that you can submit more evidence after filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for legal help and use docket examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Some environmental law groups, university law clinics, or legal aid organizations represent people pro bono; EPA’s External Civil Rights docket includes links to complaints and can help you find lawyers doing this work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many complaints that led to agreements were filed by lawyers, but some were not. Lawyers who have never filed a Title VI complaint might not be the best fit; reading well-organized complaints can provide practical templates and tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-file and consider other agencies (Department of Justice and others)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the entity taking discriminatory actions isn’t an EPA funding recipient, or if multiple agencies fund the entity, consider filing with other federal agencies and cross-filing with the Department of Justice’s Civil Rights Division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The DOJ accepts complaints and will review them to determine next steps; some people ask DOJ to coordinate investigations even if DOJ isn’t a funder. Many federal agencies have Title VI regulations and under the current administration are supposed to prioritize environmental justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider other legal avenues and local advocacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Some groups have addressed discriminatory pollution by filing lawsuits (often under environmental laws rather than Title VI), and local advocacy (running for office, teaming with researchers, participating in advisory councils) can effect change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court has limited private Title VI suits to cases of intentional discrimination, making environmental-law litigation or constitutional claims (e.g., Equal Protection) alternative paths. Engage with EPA and White House advisory councils and local planning processes as additional levers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete examples of triggering actions and harms
rubrics_metrics.description: Permits, zoning decisions, enforcement inconsistencies, failure to provide interpreters at public meetings, or failure to install/maintain infrastructure (e.g., storm drains) are examples of agency actions or omissions that can constitute discriminatory acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think about whether an agency action allowed pollution to increase in an overburdened area, whether enforcement differs across communities, or whether resource allocation discriminates. These concrete examples can anchor your allegations and start the 180-day clock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the process and be persistent
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing an EPA complaint is a process that requires following procedural steps and sustained effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stick with it, track EPA’s online docket, ask to be included in resolution efforts, and sustain pressure (including public and local action) to move agencies toward transparency, accountability, and responsiveness.
